analysis.title: Global Views: Downside Growth Risks
key_insights: Global and G3 growth in 2026 is running in line with GS estimates of potential GDP. Fiscal easing and the AI boom offset the drag from the war in Iran and higher US tariffs.
GS standing forecasts project more of the same growth in 2027 as lower energy prices offset fading fiscal and AI tailwinds, but the balance of risks is to the downside.

Energy prices have climbed sharply again on fears of renewed Middle East escalation. Gasoline, diesel, jet fuel and European/Asian natural gas are near or above their March/April highs, which weighs on consumers and energy-importing economies.

Longer-term yields have risen about 100bp on average across DM curves since early 2026, driven by large deficits, AI-linked borrowing and central bank hikes. If sustained, GS estimates a cumulative 0.6% drag on GDP via housing, consumer durables and business investment. Only part of this drag is in standing forecasts because GS expects yields to pull back.

The AI investment growth impulse was set to peak in late 2026 or early 2027, before sustainability concerns intensified in recent weeks. AI investment as a share of GDP is expected to grow more slowly over the next year, and the boost from last year's US depreciation allowances is fading, weighing on US capex growth.

AI-driven stock gains added an estimated 0.4pp (0.25% of GDP) to US consumer spending growth over the past year. The effect should decline gradually if stocks match GS strategists' forecasts and more sharply if AI-related stocks keep falling.

AI adoption is starting to show up in labor data beyond tech. Across US nonmanufacturing industries, firm-level AI adoption has a statistically significant negative correlation with employment growth and a positive correlation with unemployment.

The Fed's signals from Williams, Jefferson and Warsh effectively rule out a hike on October 28. GS still expects a 25bp hike to 4-4.25% on December 9 because spot inflation is too high. Risks to GS's 2027 disinflation forecast are to the upside, mainly in energy, and higher inflation could bring another hike in March. GS still sees cuts in late 2027/early 2028.

The ECB is expected to hold next week and deliver a final hike to 2.75% in December. French bond market turbulence adds downside risk to that call, and has tightened financial conditions enough to cut ¼-½pp from annualized growth in coming quarters.

A December ECB hike could be read as insufficient focus on euro area fragmentation if French turbulence intensifies. Pairing a hike with renewed balance sheet expansion is possible, but the hurdle is high because buying French bonds raises moral hazard concerns about fiscal adjustment.

GS expects the Bank of England to raise Bank Rate 25bp to 4% on November 5. UK GDP has surprised to the upside this year and unemployment fell to 4.7% in August on a 3-month average basis (1-month rate 4.1%). Market pricing of 4+ hikes including November looks excessive. GS also expects hikes in Canada and New Zealand this week and Australia next week.

GS raised its 2026 China GDP forecast to 4.6% after slightly faster Q3 growth, but most activity indicators are weak. Property activity and fixed asset investment are contracting y/y, and large retailers still post substantial y/y sales declines. Hitting the 4.5-5% official target needs ever-larger trade surpluses, already at 1% of global GDP, which raises the risk of trade barriers against Chinese exports.

GS's strongest global view is that central banks will deliver fewer hikes than priced. Rates strategists see underweight positioning, diminished technical risks and risk-asset pressure as reasons the recent rally could extend.

GS equity strategists are wary of momentum factor exposure given narrow breadth, but expect the S&P 500 to resume climbing after the midterm election on solid earnings growth. Credit strategists stay cautious on IG technology bonds but see scope for a near-term reversal in HY after the recent selloff.

GS FX strategists expect the yen to hedge further AI jitters, partly because such jitters would shrink US-Japan rate differentials. Commodity strategists recommend targeted exposure to oil products and European natural gas as escalation hedges, plus longer-term copper, gold and select power market exposure.

charts_described: Exhibit 6 shows GS Fed funds scenarios: two hikes with later cuts to 3.25-3.5% (GS baseline, 50%), three hikes with a higher terminal rate (35%), and recession (15%).
Exhibit 4 shows a US wealth-effect scenario analysis on real PCE growth: AI stocks up 55% and other stocks up 20% (upside), baseline, and AI stocks down 40% and other stocks down 15% (downside).
Exhibit 5 shows a regression of employment growth on AI adoption of -0.3 - 0.09 * AI adoption (t-stat -2.07) and unemployment rate of -2 + 0.09 * AI adoption (t-stat 4.20).

tension_points.bull_case: GS base case is that AI investment pays off in higher productivity and economywide profits, and strategists expect the S&P 500 to resume climbing after the midterm election on solid earnings growth.
tension_points.bear_case: The AI growth impulse is peaking, a decline in AI stocks would sharply reduce the consumer wealth effect, and AI adoption is correlated with weaker employment growth and higher unemployment outside tech.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Continued declines in AI-related stocks, which would cut the wealth effect more sharply (downside scenario: AI stocks down 40%).

tension_points.bull_case: Central banks deliver fewer hikes than priced, so yields pull back and the recent rally extends.
tension_points.bear_case: Higher energy prices push inflation up, leading to another Fed hike in March and a higher terminal rate.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Energy-driven upside inflation surprises that lead to a hike in March.
